routes.description: Establish the resurrection as the most probable explanation of the accepted historical facts under ordinary criteria of historical inference.
routes.successCriteria: The historical premises must be sufficiently established, resurrection must explain them collectively, and skeptical alternatives and prior-probability objections must not prevent the comparative inference.

motionBridge.description: The resurrection must emerge as the most probable overall explanation of the relevant historical facts.

centralBridges.description: The crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciples must have adequate historical support.
The resurrection hypothesis must explain the historical facts with greater collective scope and power than naturalistic alternatives.
The resurrection must remain probabilistically eligible when assessed within an independently supported theistic context.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical proof must permit probabilistic inference rather than require mathematical demonstration.
Early and independent traditions must support the appearance reports against a late-legend account.

routes.description: Show that evidential standards, prior probability, source uncertainty, or viable natural explanations prevent resurrection from becoming the warranted best explanation.
routes.successCriteria: At least one indispensable premise or comparative inference must remain insufficiently supported, or skeptical alternatives must remain preferable given the claim's prior probability and evidential demands.

motionBridge.description: The available evidence must remain insufficient to warrant resurrection as the best historical explanation.

centralBridges.description: The evidential threshold must reflect the resurrection claim's extraordinary character and asserted divine significance.
Naturalistic accounts must remain credible enough to block an inference from their imperfections to resurrection.
Uncertainty or development in the appearance traditions must weaken confidence in the facts requiring supernatural explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The low prior probability assigned to divine intervention must be included in the comparative assessment.
Public empirical defeaters must be capable of overriding contrary experiential religious warrant.

sectionSelections.title: Experiential warrant and empirical defeaters
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue defines whether personal religious experience can warrant belief and how public historical or empirical evidence constrains that warrant.

proSelections.proposition: Personal experience of God can rationally ground Christian belief without supporting argument, though belief must ultimately conform to genuine facts.
Conclusive identification of Jesus's remains would falsify the resurrection, but archaeological uncertainty makes that scenario unlikely and current historical evidence instead supports resurrection.

conSelections.proposition: Decisive empirical evidence against the resurrection would defeat any contrary warrant supplied by personal religious experience.
Historical inquiry establishes facts surrounding the alleged resurrection, while resurrection itself remains an inference about their best explanation rather than a directly proved fact.

sectionSelections.title: Evidential standard for an extraordinary claim
sectionSelections.rationale: The required standard determines when probabilistic historical evidence can warrant a uniquely consequential supernatural conclusion.

proSelections.proposition: Establishing resurrection as the most probable historical explanation constitutes proof in the ordinary historical sense, even without mathematical demonstration.
Ordinary evidence can establish an extraordinary event when that evidence is much more probable if the event occurred than if it did not.

conSelections.proposition: The resurrection's extraordinary nature, moral importance, and asserted divine purpose justify requiring substantially stronger evidence than ordinary historical claims require.
A God who strongly wants humanity to believe in the resurrection should provide more evidence than the roughly ordinary historical record available.

sectionSelections.title: Prior probability and theistic context
sectionSelections.rationale: Comparative explanation depends on whether divine resurrection begins with a prohibitive prior probability or becomes plausible within a supported theistic context.

proSelections.proposition: Miracles are not intrinsically implausible if God exists, so resurrection evidence should be assessed within the theistic context supplied by independent arguments for a creator.

conSelections.proposition: Even weak naturalistic alternatives may remain more credible for an atheist because divine resurrection has an exceptionally unfavorable prior probability.

sectionSelections.title: Historical facts and naturalistic explanation
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue contains the central inference from the proposed historical facts and tests whether a natural psychological account can explain the same material without resurrection.

proSelections.proposition: Crucifixion, burial, the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and transformed disciples are widely accepted historical facts best explained by resurrection under standard explanatory criteria.
Hallucination lacks explanatory power because Jewish expectations would not yield belief in an isolated resurrection, and it lacks scope because it does not explain the empty tomb.

conSelections.proposition: The disciples could sincerely suffer for a mistaken belief, with grief-induced hallucination providing a natural explanation for their conviction that Jesus had risen.

sectionSelections.title: Attestation and legendary development
sectionSelections.rationale: Confidence in the resurrection inference depends on whether appearance traditions are early and independent or instead display uncertain attestation and progressive legendary elaboration.

proSelections.proposition: Postmortem experiences are supported by early Pauline tradition, multiple Gospel attestations, broad scholarly acceptance, and Mark's foreshadowing of appearances.
The dates of completed Gospels do not date their sources, and independent early traditions behind the Gospels and Paul weigh against late legendary development.

conSelections.proposition: Group appearances have sparse and uneven attestation, while the earliest Gospel narrates no post-resurrection appearance, weakening confidence in the underlying reports.
The Gospel sequence suggests legendary development as Mark gives only a prediction and later Gospels add increasingly numerous and elaborate appearance episodes.
